how-much-to-charge-to-install-a-skylight.text:
← Skylight install bid calculator

How much to charge to install a skylight

Roofers and window crews get shopped on a published $800 a skylight installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the unit or the opening. One tubular sun tunnel dropped into an existing chase is a different job from three solar-venting glass units with new cut-ins, tile flashing, drywall light shafts, and a second-story ladder.

Open the free skylight install bid calculator

Price the unit and the opening, not the $800 dump

A skylight is a unit, then an opening, then the roof it sits in. A tubular sun tunnel is a 10–14" tube. Fixed glass is a curb unit with no vent. Solar or electric venting is the remote and a rain sensor. Replace-existing pulls the old unit. New cut-in opens the roof and the ceiling.

A tube drop is not a venting cut-in

The cheap special is almost always one tubular unit, replace-existing, asphalt, no shaft, one story. A solar-venting tile cut-in with three shafts is a different crew day. Matching a per-unit number on that job is how a sold opening becomes a loss when the shaft and the flashing eat the margin.

This is not a window, a reroof, or a solar array

Window replacement is wall openings and united inches. An asphalt shingle reroof is squares and pitch. Metal roof is standing-seam panels. Solar PV is dollars per watt. A sunroom is glazed walls. A screened porch is mesh. This prices a skylight: unit count, type, scope, roof, and extras.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the skylight install bid calculator. It is not a roofing specification, a flashing design, a building-code determination, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install a skylight?

Charge from unit count, type, scope, roof, and extras — not a published $800 / unit special. One tubular sun tunnel dropped into an existing chase is a different job from three solar-venting glass units with new cut-ins, tile flashing, drywall light shafts, and a second-story ladder.

Is a tubular sun tunnel the same bid as a venting glass skylight?

No. A tubular sun tunnel is a 10–14 inch tube in a chase — that is the cheap special. Fixed glass is a curb unit with no vent. Solar or electric venting adds a remote, a rain sensor, and a heavier curb. Matching a tube number on a venting cut-in is how a sold opening becomes a loss when the shaft and the flashing eat the margin.

How do a new cut-in, tile flashing, and a light shaft change a skylight price?

Replace-existing pulls the old unit and reuses a sound curb. New cut-in opens the roof and the ceiling and frames the hole. Asphalt takes a standard flashing kit. Tile or metal is specialty flashing. Low-slope is a built curb. Drywall shafts, ice-and-water, laminated glass, shaft paint, and a second story do not live in a published per-unit dump.

Is this the same as window replacement, a reroof, or solar panels?

No. Window replacement is wall openings and united inches. An asphalt shingle reroof is squares and pitch. Metal roof is standing-seam panels. Solar PV is dollars per watt. A sunroom is glazed walls. This prices a skylight: unit count, type, scope, roof, and extras.

    Common questions

    Why is the shaft $0 on the default job?

    Because the defaults replace an existing tubular unit, and a replacement re-uses the opening and the light shaft that are already there. Shaft hours and material only appear when you enter shafts — which a new installation through a finished ceiling always needs, along with framing, drywall, and paint. That single difference is most of the gap between a $1,379.84 replacement and a new cut-in.

    Why is flashing billed separately from the skylight?

    Because it is matched to the roof, not to the unit: the default adds $85 of flashing against a $380 unit. Flashing kits differ by roof covering, and fitting one to tile or metal takes materially longer than to asphalt. Nearly every skylight leak traced back to installation is a flashing failure rather than a failed unit, which is why it is a visible line here rather than folded into the unit price.

    Why is travel $22.40 on top of the travel-and-equipment charge?

    Because they cover different things. The per-mile line is the vehicle running cost for the eight default miles; the separate travel-and-equipment charge is the fixed cost of turning out at all. The trip also appears a third time, as 1.68 hours of paid crew time. Short-duration roof work is dominated by the cost of showing up — the whole job is only 7.28 hours.

    Does an existing roof warranty survive this?

    Possibly not, and the tool cannot tell you. Cutting a new penetration in a roof still under a manufacturer or workmanship warranty frequently voids it unless the original roofer does the work. Check before you quote a cut-in on a recent roof: it is a common reason a homeowner cancels after accepting a price, and it is cheaper to find out first.

should-i-install-a-customer-supplied-sky.text:
← Skylight install bid calculator

Should I install a customer-supplied skylight?

Homeowners call with a box already in the garage: “I found one on Amazon for $180. Can you just install it for $350?” That reads as free margin because the unit invoice left the bid. It did not take the pull, the cut, the flashing, or the chance that a boxed unit is sized for a curb you do not have.

Open the free skylight install bid calculator

Zeroing the unit is not a free install

A contractor-supplied tubular replace on asphalt, one story, still carries the unit and flashing invoices along with the labor. An owner-supplied unit that actually fits zeros those two material lines and keeps the same pull, cut, and site hours. On a typical cheap special — $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, 8 miles — the contractor-supplied walk-away is about $1,018. Zeroing the unit and flashing invoice drops that to about $483, but a $350 install-only ask still loses about $133 once labor, travel, and overhead are counted. A unit that turns out to be the wrong size adds an inspect trip and a hardware kit, and the walk-away climbs back to about $646 — the $350 ask now loses about $296.

You supplyThey supply, it fitsThey supply, wrong unit

Walk-away on the cheap specialAbout $1,018About $483About $646

Wrong unit is a second trip

Online listings skip the curb measurement and the roof pitch. Boxes come sized for a curb-mount opening when the roof needs a deck-mount kit, or a tubular kit shows up missing the diffuser or the right run of tubing. Setting the wrong unit means a second dispatch plus flashing or hardware they expect you to eat. Price that callback on the same opening before you agree. The numbers above add a second inspect trip and a small hardware kit on top of the rates you already typed.

How to use the comparison

Open the skylight install bid calculator, enter the opening you are standing on, zero the unit and flashing invoices, and put their install-only number in “price you’re considering.” Compare the walk-away price you get against you-supply, owner-supplies-it-fits, and owner-supplies-wrong-unit. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install a skylight. It is not a building-code determination, a manufacturer warranty question, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each supply path.

Common questions

Should I install a skylight the homeowner bought online?

Only after you price the job without the unit and flashing invoices. The labor, the cut or pull, the roof flashing, and overhead do not zero out. A $350 install-only special often sits under that walk-away number even when the unit itself cost you nothing.

Does a customer-supplied skylight make an install-only special profitable?

Usually not. Zeroing the unit and flashing invoice drops the bid a lot on a cheap tubular unit, but loaded labor, roof flashing, travel, and overhead stay. On a typical replace-existing tubular job the owner-supplied walk-away is still well above a $350 install-only ask.

What if the unit they bought does not fit the opening?

That is a second trip plus a hardware or flashing kit they did not budget for — a boxed unit sized for a different curb, or a tubular kit missing the right diffuser. Price that callback on the same opening before you agree to install whatever showed up in their garage.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-skylight-special.html.text:
← Skylight Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat "$800 a skylight" special

"$800 a skylight installed" is not a price for a skylight install — it is a price for one specific unit type, scope, and roof, quietly applied to every opening the truck pulls up to.

What a flat per-skylight special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a postcard or a website, read off and repeated. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually the cheapest unit type (a tubular sun tunnel dropped into an existing chase), replacing an existing curb, standard asphalt flashing, no drywall shaft, single story — and then reused for every skylight afterward, whether or not the next opening looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the unit count and type — tubular sun tunnel, fixed glass, or solar venting — whether the job replaces an existing unit or is a new roof cut-in, the roof (asphalt, tile or metal, or low-slope), how many drywall light shafts it needs, extras such as ice-and-water shield, laminated glass, or interior shaft paint, story count, travel, and your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the unit, the cut-in and framing, the roof flashing, and the shaft work separately, and returns a walk-away price and an extra-work share below which the job loses money — for this roof, not a generic one.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same headline price whether the job is a tubular sun tunnel into an existing chase or a solar-venting glass unit with a new cut-in — several times the unit cost and labor for the same word "skylight". Prices the unit from the entered type, scope, and roof, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "a skylight" as one drop-in, with no separate line for cutting the roof deck, framing the opening, or building a drywall light shaft down to the ceiling. Times cutting, framing, and shaft labor as their own extra-work hours, so that work shows up instead of being absorbed into the unit price or skipped.
Assumes standard asphalt flashing and no shaft, so a tile or metal roof, a low-slope curb, or a painted drywall shaft gets quoted the same as one that needs none of that. Adds specialty roof flashing and shaft hours only for the roof and shaft count entered, so the two jobs price differently.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the tech a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when an owner asks to match a cheaper tube quote on a venting cut-in. Reports the walk-away price and the extra-work share of the job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the tech commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-skylight special get the price wrong?

Because the labor and material scale with unit type, scope, and roof, not with the word "skylight" alone. A tubular sun tunnel dropped into an existing chase on a single-story asphalt roof is a different job from a solar-venting glass unit needing a new roof cut-in, tile flashing, a drywall light shaft, and a second-story ladder. A flat special quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat special usually leave out entirely?

The extra work a new cut-in drags in on top of the unit itself: cutting the roof deck, framing the opening, building the drywall light shaft, and running it up through a second story. A rate built around "install a skylight" has nowhere to put those hours, so a tech pricing off the special alone is short before the ladder goes up.

What happens when the roof or the shaft changes the job?

A flat installed rate assumes standard asphalt flashing and no light shaft. Tile or metal roofing needs specialty flashing, a low-slope roof needs a built curb and extra waterproofing, and any new cut-in usually means framing and painting a drywall shaft down to the ceiling. Each of those is its own material and labor line a rate never asked about, charged the same price for a job that takes longer and costs more.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote a skylight install?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same unit type, replacing an existing curb, standard asphalt, no shaft, single story — a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard rate does not know which band a given roof is in and neither does the tech until the walkthrough.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, equipment cost, or what competitors charge. It takes the unit type, scope, roof, shafts, extras, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price and extra-work share for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-skylight special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a roofing or remodeling company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this skylight install cost, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — roofing, general contracting, HVAC, plumbing, and remodeling among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Public research puts its founding in 2011, headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and reports it is used by more than 200,000 service professionals. Its own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home service field service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing, and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a skylight install should cost from unit count, type, and the roof cut before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a crew across a season, or collect a payment. It takes a skylight install — unit count, tubular versus fixed versus solar-venting, replace-existing versus a new roof cut-in, asphalt versus tile, metal, or low-slope roofing, a laminated or ice-and-water shaft, and extras — plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a copyable customer-facing bid summary, a saved bid that reopens on the next visit, a shareable bid link, and a printable customer proposal with scope lines, a deposit split, and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
